title: Multiplication 085
reflection: Working with range for a over [1, K^1/3] and b over [a, K^1/2] gave TLE, so ranged over a [1, K^1/3] and b over [a, (K/a)^1/2] which was good enough I guess, ranging b over [a, (K/a)^1/2] also ensures that c >= b, because b seeks to qualify as the smaller factor of (K / a).
approach: I know a cannot be greater than K^1/3 (else a*b*c would exceed K) and b cannot exceed K^1/2 (else b*c would exceed K), so I can just brute force over the domain for a and b, and check feasibility and increment the count if ok.

past_attempts.approach: Since in the triplet a <= b <= c, I realize that a cannot be greater than K^1/3 (otherwise a*b*c > K), and similarly b cannot be greater than K^1/2 (otherwise b*c > K). But I am struggling to see how can I efficiently brute for it. As of now, I have considered looping over the range [1, N^1/3] for a, looping over the range [1, N^1/3] for b, but the count is conditional. I have also considered subset split, since in the prime-factorization of K, there can be atmost 40 (2^40) primes contributing, I can try to split the 40 entries into three groups and then calculate each groups product, but this too is leadnign no where.

notes.note: Chose: bounds a ≤ K^(1/3), b ≤ √(K/a), c forced by division — 1.5·10^8 pairs, AC in 9:10 cold, 35/35 hidden. Needed (sharper): restrict the candidates to divisors of K, cost τ(K)²/2. Gap was recognition, not implementation: the bound plan was abandoned at 39 min without ever evaluating 1.5·K^(2/3) = 1.5·10^8 (0.23 s); the equation's candidate set (a·b | K → a,b divide K) went unexplored, and the divisor thought surfaced only as a 3^40 prime-partition.

title: Multiplication 085 — divisor version
reflection: Tried by reducing the search over the divisors of K, which is O(tau(K)^2), which works for K <= 1e12, since tau(K) < 7000, doable.

notes.note: Chose: divisor enumeration in O(√K) with the i*i<=K guard and i!=K/i dedupe, sort, pair loop with c forced and divide-first to avoid the 10^24 product — 12:25 AC, 35/35 hidden, no hints. Wrote the estimate into the code as `assert(DIV_COUNT <= 6720)`, and stated the cost in the right variable in the reflection (O(τ(K)²)). Recognition now matches the card.

title: Digit Product Equation
reflection: Had to figure out that, most of the searches will be doomed to be wrong, so instead of starting from candidates for m and checking if they meet the criteria, we start from the range of possibilities of f(m) which has much smaller search space and then check the condition.

notes.note: Chose: invert the equation — enumerate the possible values of f (box 2^a3^b5^c7^d), m = B + k, accept iff f(m) == k, with k = 0 handled as m = B; every loop guard uses k ≤ N − B. Needed: the same idea, and it was reached cold in one message before any code. Gap was neither: the two slips were in the box's own definition (missed prime 7; exponent bounds taken from 10 digits instead of 11) and both were caught by sample 1 / the constraint before coding. AC first submission, 37/37 hidden, 15:00.

title: CF545D - Queue
reflection: Had to realize while implementation that, if even in the optimum order if certain customer is dissatisfied, then let's just put them at the end, we are going to get the same result, but putting them at the end eases the waiting time of others.
approach: This is just greedy, people who require less serve-time are willing to wait less time and give us the same reward to the total (+1), if there an optimal solution where in the queue at index i, we have i < j, but t_i > t_j, we can swap them and still retain valid order and the same result. So we can always work with sorted order.

notes.note: Ch3 checkpoint, cold and blind: approach line written before code was chapter 3's sentence verbatim — exchange argument (i<j, t_i>t_j → swap is safe) then sort, then one running quantity. 8:25, first submission, no hints. Recognition matched the card with no label on it.

title: ABC115 D - Christmas
reflection: Recursion with some partial memoization, I was unsure if naked recursion without "patties" memoized result would fit in time limit.
approach: I am thinking to with recursion on this one. Each burger will have the size of f(L) = 1 + f(L) + 1 + f(L) + 1, and the number of patties will be fp(L) = fp(L - 1) + 1 + fp(L - 1), I will use recursion to collect number of patties, I feel it's going to be a lot of intersection so I will compute the fp(L) for L = 1 till 50 beforehand using DP.

notes.note: Ch1 checkpoint: approach line was right (layers[L]=2L+3, patties[L]=2P+1, descend the five blocks) but took 37:40 against a 20:00 budget. Gap was implementation-side and was a cost question never asked: "will naked recursion fit" was answered by memoising (the table is constants, nothing repeats) instead of by counting calls. The walk is a path — level drops by one per call, ≤ ~100 calls at L=50, 1 call for a full burger. AC first submission; 30 of those minutes were the un-counted recursion.

title: CF816B - Karen and Coffee
reflection: Time complexity is O(T + N + Q). T <= MAXT.
approach: Each recipe has a defined range of temperature which is suitable, so this is a range update, which I will perform using difference-array followed by a single sweep. And then we have enquiry on the valid number of temperature within the range, we note that between the queries the search-space is not changing, we can form a one-time prefix-sum array and query on top of it.

notes.note: Ch2 checkpoint: difference array on the recipe ranges, one sweep to coverage, a second prefix to a count array, then O(1) per query — the chapter's sentence end to end. 9:00, first submission. Approach line even named the right reason ("the search space is not changing between queries").

title: LCS
reflection: Standard LCS solution with reconstruction. One cool thing, the reconstruction can stop immediately once we encounter dp[f][s] = 0.
approach: I know this typical DP problem, here the state is (i, j), f(i, j) = LCS value having considered first i character of first string and first j characters of the second. at each point (i, j) we either drop the character from the first so we consult (i - 1, j) or we drop from the second string (i, j - 1) or if first[i] == second[j] then we have an additional option to consider 1 + f(i - 1, j - 1). I see though we require to construct the solution, so we will start from f(N, M) and then check (i - 1, j), (i, j - 1) and (i - 1, j - 1) + 1, we travel from (N, M) and check three options whichever has lent the actual value, we move to that cell and repeat until we reach (0, 0)

notes.note: Ch4 cold: approach line before code had state (i,j) over prefix lengths, three-branch transition, and a backward walk from (N,M) — recognition matched the card with no hints, 16:19, first submission. Needed: exactly that. Code was tighter than the written plan: instead of "whichever of the three lent the value", it drops from s if the value survives, else from t, else takes the match under an assert — a priority order that cannot be ambiguous. Slack, not error.

title: String
reflection: I ran the loop for (a = 0; a < A; a++) I don't need to compute a = A, I could've but that would require some if-guards on the s1[a] and it's wasnt' required so I didn't put in the effort.
approach: Working with f(i, a, b, c) = Having constructed T of length i, which has a subsequence which matches the a-prefix of S1, b-prefix of S2 and c-prefix of S3, we try to add new character and indepedently check a' = a + (S1[a] == new-character), similarly for b and c. And contribute to that state. The base-case should be f(0, 0, 0, 0) = 1 and other states state with identity element which is zero.

notes.note: Ch4 invention, cold: state (i,a,b,c) = layer plus greedy reach into each forbidden pattern, proposed at the board before any confirmation, transition a'=a+(S1[a]==x) per pattern, read-out a sum over the open box. Needed: exactly that. 33:25, first submission, no hints. Two design choices were his: keeping a==A out of the loop so the absorbing state is never materialised (valid because subsequence-containment is monotone), and the sum-over-box read-out rather than one cell. Not-yet-seen: the 26-letter inner loop collapses to k weighted writes + one for the other 26-k.

title: Dynasty Puzzles
reflection: I had to recover twice, once from MLE, when I realized I don't need to hold all the layers, I only need two. so the state f(idx, s, e) became just cur(s, e), nxt(s, e), this resolved MLE, but then I faced TLE, it was because I was iterating over all 26 possibilities of s and all 26 possibilities of e. When I was rejecting most of the matches because e != _s, for each (s, e) I know I can directly pick the state (s, _s) since only that can contribute anything at all, this would handle the "take" choice, but there was another choice "don't take" for that I need the max_self(nxt[s][e], curr[s][e]) transition, but then I realized, if at the start of the iteration instead of taking nxt(30, vector<int>(30, -INF)) if I start with nxt = curr, then the initial values are already set to curr which has handled the case of "not take". Got lucky twice I was able to strike the deal.
approach: I realize for each selection I only care about the starting-character and the ending character of the selection made. f(i, s, e) = longest name that can be formed having considered first i names, where the first name has the first character is 's' and the last name has the last character as 'e'. Towards the end we can readout from f(N, s, s) for each s = 'a' to 'z'.

notes.note: Checkpoint 1 rep: chose (i, start-letter, end-letter) — state named correctly on the first approach line, no hints. Needed: exactly that. Gap was execution, not recognition: attempt 1 MLE (full N+1 layer table of 30x30 = 1.8 GB that the read-out never touches), attempt 2 TLE (676-cell scan per name plus a per-name assign), attempt 3 AC 35:28 after cutting to 26 writes — only column _s is read. Both recoveries came from one question, 'which cells does this cell read', asked after two failures instead of before coding. Third fix was the good one: nxt starts as a copy of curr, so 'don't take' is the default rather than a branch.

title: Ayoub and Lost Array
reflection: I had to find the number of elements that leaving remainder k, and lie between [l, r], it was adhoc, but easy.
approach: I realize I actually don't care about the sum of the elements but the sum (mod3), which can only take 3 values, 0, 1, 2. So I will work with state (i, mod), f(i, mod) = number of ways to place i elements such that their sum leaves remainder mod (mod3), for each state (i, mod) we will try to add number in range [l, r] at the last, we actually don't need to add all [l, r] we only need to now how many in numbers between [l, r] are belong to the bucket num (mod 3) = 0, 1, 2, since during the sum (mod 3) we only care num (mod 3), so we can find how many number between [l, r] leave remainder = 0, 1, 2, let's call it k0, k1, k2, now for each state (i, mod) we will add into the state (i + 1, (mod + 0) %3). dp[i + 1][mod'] += dp[i][mod] * k0, we will do the same for each bucket 0, 1, 2.

notes.note: Checkpoint 1 rep: chose (i, sum mod 3) with the whole [l,r] input collapsed to three residue counts — state named correctly on the first approach line, no hints. Needed: exactly that. 16:45, first submission, AC. Recognition and execution both clean; the residue-count arithmetic (L--, then R/3 - L/3 style prefix counts) was right first time, which is the Ch. 3 rotation done as counting rather than as a table.

title: ABC118 B - Foods Loved by Everyone
reflection: Time complexity outside of reading the inputs is O(M)
approach: There are N, kind of people and M kinds of food, I can keep a count for each food item how many people like that food. And for a food item k, if the cnt[k] = N, then I know everyone like this food and this is a candidate to be contribute towards the total.

notes.note: Chose per-food occurrence counts + tally cnt==N (accumulate, not intersect); exactly the needed idea. Recognition clean, implementation clean — 4:02.

title: ABC183 D - Water Heater
reflection: Since the time range can start from t = 0, usage[t] has to be non-negative, since in a valid range, nothing can end on t = 0, without starting on or before zero.
approach: We only have one heater, at every minute i, there is a certain demand, we need to check if demand in each minute is within the capacity. Now when the person bathes for [Si, Ti) and uses Pi per minute, the usage for the range [Si, Ti) increments by Pi, it's a range update. And we see that the enquiry is only once at the very end, so we can work with difference-array, for each [Si, Ti) we can put delta in the usage_this_minute[Si] += Pi and usage_this_minute[Ti] -=p and the after all the deltas are put, before the enquiry I run a sweep, and during enquiry I check if for all minutes, the usage <= W.

notes.note: Chose difference array with -P at T_i (half-open respected, long long totals) — the needed idea, transferred straight from cf_816B. Clean, first attempt at 12:26.

title: CF292B - Network Topology
reflection: Since the graph is connected each node should have a positive degree, added an assert on that.
approach: The problem statement directly reveals what needs to be done, check the degrees of each node and then it reduces to merely an if-else loop check the original problem-statement from the judge didn't have mention of "degree", though I would have been able to derive it anyway.

notes.note: Chose degree histogram (separate counters for deg 1 / 2 / N-1) so the three shapes fall out of the counts — the needed reduction; note the sub-cases follow from the counts, no m-check needed. Clean at 20:57, though the statement named "degree" itself, so recognition was largely handed over.

title: CF327A - Flipping Game
reflection: I could have implemented Kadane, which would have removed the need for readout, but this is fine too.
approach: I would introduce a concept of "excess-of-zero" for each sub-array I will define excess-of-zero as number-of-zero - number-of-one in that subarray, I would find the subarray with largest excess and flip the bits for that subarray, gaining the "excess-of-zero" value to the total. Implementation could be dp, dp(i) = subarray with maximum excess ending at index i. and then I readout the maximum value for each i. Actually N <= 100, ridiculously small I can even run a brute-force, but I am going to stick with O(N).

notes.note: Chose excess = zeros - ones plus a dp over the segment's right endpoint with a non-empty base, so the "exactly one move" case falls out — the needed reduction, and the trap was recognised before coding. Clean at 28:20.

title: ABC177 C - Sum of product of pairs
reflection: Had to realize I was double counting, so the final count had to be halved.
approach: To find the sum of product of two terms at a time, I can consider them as (a1 + a2 + a3 ...) * (a1 + a2 + a3 ...) - a1^2 - a2^2 - a3^2 ... So basically product of the sum - sum of squares.

notes.note: Chose (S² − Σa²)/2 with inv(2) mod p, not integer halving — exactly the needed idea, and the floor-halving trap was avoided; 7:21 included building a reusable modular-arithmetic toolbox.

title: CSES 1652 - Forest Queries
reflection: I am curious to see if such exclusion inclusion problems can be done with push-DP, I don't think push-DP fits well with such problems. Need to actually know when push-DP shines and when pull-DP takes the cake.
approach: For any arbitrary rectangle in the grid I need to calculate the number of trees inside it. Since the queries are huge I cannot compute the tree count adhoc. Let me work with wishful thinking, let's say I know for each cell (i, j) the number of trees in the rectangle with top-left corner at (0, 0) and bottom right at (i, j). Now to compute the answer for (a, b) at top-left and (c, d) at bottom-right. I can work with inclusion-exclusion result = dp(c, d) - dp(a - 1, d) - dp(c, b - 1) + dp(a - 1, b - 1). Now what remains is to calculate dp(i, j) efficiently which also can be calculated efficinelty with dp(i, j) = dp(i - 1, j) + dp(i, j - 1) - dp(i - 1, j - 1) + (grid[i][j] == '*'). So this should do it in O(N^2 + Q)

notes.note: Chose 2D prefix via inclusion-exclusion, both build and query, with y-before-x field order correct — the needed reduction. 13:17 (95% of budget); open question was push vs pull form.

title: ABC178 D - Redistribution
reflection: I tried a prune with "if (dp[s] == 0) continue", but doubt it's of any major help.
approach: I am thinking of simple DP on this one, dp(s) = number of ways to split the sum into sequences. Now that we have the sum 's' covered we will try to add next term v = {3, ... k} such that s + k <= S and increment the value of dp(s + v) += dp(s), this requires O(S^2) with S <= 2000 it should be doable.

notes.note: Chose push-form DP (from each sum, extend by every term ≥ 3), which makes dp[1]=dp[2]=0 fall out of the direction — the needed idea with the base case got for free. Clean at 28:51 clock.

title: ABC147 C - HonestOrUnkind2
reflection: The implementation was particularly tricky I got lured into having is_honest as bit-number, when the opinion of a person p1 may skip any comment about person p2, so just two states weren't enough to capture all possibilities of testimony.
approach: My first thought is just brute force, all the combinations of the state for P is 2^N and then for each of such configuration I have to run N^2 tests, so the total would be O(N^2 * 2^N) with N <= 15, should be doable

notes.note: Chose 2^N enumeration with a -1 "no opinion" sentinel in the testimony matrix — the sentinel was the real content, since two states cannot express silence. Clean, 22:22 = 93% of its per-problem budget, the round's only near-limit solve.

title: Candies
reflection: I took some time in realizing the DP optimization is possible, I tried to look for simpler state or reduction in state, when I started looking for reduction in transition I struck gold with difference_arrays, also I got stuck in modulo arithmetic where I used naked addition in one of the loops nxt[k] += nxt[k - 1]. Costed me a few minute to realize that.
approach: I thinking for a simple state (i, k), f(i, k) = number of ways to distribute k candies amongst first i children. If I am at the state f(i, k)I will try to give the next child anywhere between [0, a_nxt] candies guarded by the fact that k + a_nxt <= K, f(i, k) would feed into f(i + 1, k + a_nxt) for all valid a_nxt. However I realize now this would lead to TLE. But I see the from each state f(i, k) we are incrementing the same value over a range of values f(i + 1, [k, min(K, a + a_nxt)]) so instead of going for each f(i + 1, t) t = [k, min(K, k + a_nxt)] for each k, I can work with difference_array + one-time sweep,  which would reduce the cost the transition cost to O(1) and then a single sweep would be O(K), so the total time complexity would be O(N * (K + K)), which is O(NK) and should fit within time limits now.

notes.note: Cold AC at CF 1700, first attempt, no hints, 32:58. Searched state reduction first (found nothing), then found the lever in the transition: each state paints a range, so a difference array plus one sweep gives O(NK) — the chapter's move, invented. Implementation: declared `vector(K+5)` then shrank it with `assign(K+1,0)`, so the end marker at index K+1 was written out of bounds (aborts under _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS; survived on the judge on leftover capacity). Also bypassed his own `add()` helper in the sweep, costing minutes.

title: ABC156 C - Rally
reflection: Realization that P has to belong within the range of X is important.
approach: Though I can think about whether I can find the optimum meeting point directly, perhaps median or something, but given the constraints N <= 100 and Xi <= 100, I can just brute force it with two for loops. One point to add here, let X_min be the smallest X_i and X_max be the largest, it doesn't make sense for P to be outside of the range of [X_min, X_max] since if there is any optimal meeting point outside of this, I can just shift that towards the and reduce the required stamina.

notes.note: Chose brute force over P in [1,100] with the "optimum lies inside [min X, max X]" argument — exactly the needed reduction (squares make median wrong); 5:50 of pure execution, recognition and implementation both clean.

title: ABC089 C - March
reflection: I realized later, I worked with a fancy next_permutation which would work generally for all NCK, but for this problem just three for loops were enough. I need to recognize nested for-loops as valid NCK selections!
approach: I can form the buckets for M, A, R, C, H, with eahc bucket containing the candidate-names starting with that character, then since I have choose three of the 5 buckets at a time, I would simulate choosing of 3 buckets and the number of ways to choose 1 person each for each bucket, which would be n(fst) * n(sec) * n(thrid). and then I do this for all selections. The only thing I need to do is simulate selection of 3 buckets from 5 buckets effectively.

notes.note: Chose five letter buckets + next_permutation to pick 3 of 5 — right reduction (10 triple products, 64-bit) but the selection machinery ate the entire budget (12:59/13:00); three nested loops were the right tool. Recognition the idea, over-engineering the enumeration.

title: CF743B - Chloe and the sequence
reflection: I skipped the hidden-tests because the neovim was freezing, perhaps too many tests. I did some mistake in passing the parameters to the recursive functions, took me some time to find the bug.
approach: This is typical layers+rank problem, recursion should work here, for each layer-k the central piece is k, layer-1 = 1, layer-2 = (layer-1)[2](layer-1), layer-3 = (layer-2)[3](layer-2). So essential f(l) = length of layer level l = 2*f(l - 1) + 1, with f(1) = 1; Now I can work with recursion here, in each recursive layer, the recursion can atmost land into first layer-k-1 or second layer-k-1, never both, so it's not going to be exponential, it would be linear contained recursion, no memoization would be needed.

notes.note: Chose block descent on layer lengths f[l]=2f[l-1]+1 — the needed reduction, derived from the structure instead of spotting the lowest-set-bit shortcut; time went to a parameter-passing bug in the recursion (17:20/19:00) and Neovim froze on 1062 tests so hidden tests were skipped. Implementation friction, idea right.

title: CF2034C - Trapped in the Witch's Labyrinth
reflection: Quite a struggle implementing the BFS. The implementation is ugly and huge and I tried to be fancy with "in_queue" if a node is already in queue, no need to add it again, which is the right idea, but when the node leaves the queue, it should've been reverted back to in_queue status as false, I kept it as true, which meant was the node ever considered, so even if the node later became accesible, I was not considering it again, which was wrong, this optimization cost me heavily, even when I knew I had to be careful with my optimization.
approach: To me this looks like a BFS problem, There would naturally be some blocks which would never be able to get out of the grid without even considering ?s, on top of the ? can also increase that count if there already some neighbour of ? which isn't freeable. If all the four neighbours of ? lead to freedom, then ? cannot cause perpetual lockage. So these are two separate problems, without considering the ?s we can run BFS on the grid and find our which cells when considered as starting cells can lead to freedom, and then we will be able to make decisions for ?s as well. BFS is a little peculiar here, because on a particular cell is deemed to be free we need to interogate the immediate four neighbours to check their feasibility, and this needs be properly contained so we don't run into infinite loops.

notes.note: Chose reverse reachability from the border plus the per-'?' rule "traps iff some in-grid neighbour is not freeable" — exactly the needed rule (AC 22/22, all discriminators passed); cost 44:42 vs 27:00 because a self-invented in_queue flag was never cleared on pop, so re-inserted cells were skipped. Recognized the idea, broke it with an optimization.

title: 063 — Monochromatic Subgrid
reflection: My initial assessment of the computation was O(2^N * HW) but I hadn't taken into account the host of keeping the count, which would be log(HW), so pessimistically it should be O(2^N HW * log(HW))

notes.note: Chose the row-subset enumeration (2^H, read off the constraint, no transpose) with a per-mask agreement test and a weighted multiplicity — folded the row count into the count (`cnt[val] += popcount(mask)`) so the A×B product could not be dropped. AC first attempt, 7:29, 17/17 hidden. Reflection costed the map's log(HW) unprompted — the algorithm/implementation split is closing.

title: 086 — Snuke's Favorite Arrays
reflection: The idea was right from the start, it took a hell lot of time to get the implementation right. Also I got stuck into one-off error, I tried for (int bit = 0; bit <= MAXB; ++bit), so in a way I was preparing a 61 bit number. I thought having an extra bit wouldn't harm with Wth 61st bit will always be zero, so there will only be a single mask "000000...N times" can contribute, 1 to the multiplication. But I was wrong since condition would only force the bits under conditions to be 0, not all bits. Also I should've realized regardless of anything I am always constructing a 60bit number the ceiling on the numbers is not coming from conditions but from the problem statement.

notes.note: Reached the right reduction before coding — 60 independent bit planes, count each by enumerating 2^N vectors against the Q rows, multiply — and expressed it as "an independent axis of length p demotes a p in the exponent to a factor p". AC first attempt, 18/18 hidden, but 44:28: the time went to a bound, not an idea (`bit <= 60` added a 61st plane assumed to contribute 1; a zero plane only pins the indices that appear in some condition, so it contributes 2^(uncovered indices)). Recognition clean, implementation friction.

Correction to the 086 note: the 61-plane off-by-one was surfaced with help, not self-caught. So the picture is narrower than "implementation friction" — the reduction was clean and unprompted, but the loop bound went unexamined until someone else looked at it.

title: Rakhsh's Revival
reflection: Had to work with addition like "carry" operation.
approach: I need to work greedy here, I can iterate from left to right and as and when I encounter a segment of m zeros, I need to apply the operation however I will apply it so that next (k - 1) characters are also turned to 1, so we fix current sgement and potentially fix the upcoming ones too.

notes.note: Chose the left-to-right scan carrying a "carry" = k-1 covered positions, firing an op the moment the zero-run hits m — exactly the needed greedy, and it placed the window as far right as possible (the placement that actually matters when k<m). AC 11:09/20:00, 29/29 hidden, hint-free. Clean.

title: KAIBUNsyo
reflection: Adopted the union-find datastructure to form the groups.
approach: First thing to realize if for any index i & (N - i) there is a conflict, as in values are different, then that has to be remediated. we can collect each such pair (a, b), (c, d), (a, e), (c, f). We realize then if we apply the operation for each disagreement palindrome can be formed however we realize if two pairs are sharing a value, for instance (a, b), (a, e), all values have to be equal (a = b = e), so essentially they form a group (a, b, e) the operations needed to make a group of size K equal is (K - 1). Since doing conflict resolution individually may lead to reversals, because we don't know which party of the two should undergo conversion. With group forming we know all other characters can be converted to one-of-them.

notes.note: Derived the transitive grouping himself — noted that resolving a mismatched pair alone risks "reversals" since you cannot tell which side converts, so pairs sharing a value force one class of size K costing K-1, then reached for union-find. Exactly the needed reduction (component size - 1, not mismatched-pair count). AC 16:34/30:00, 47/47 hidden. Clean.

title: Deque (AtCoder DP L)
reflection: Game theory with DP, realizing that both Taro and opponent are playing the same optimum game, with same domain.
approach: I realize this can be solved by DP, considering the state (i, j), f(i, j) = maximum score you can obtain over your opponent when playing first on the sequence [ai, ... , aj]. We have two choices either pick ith element or jth, since our opponent will also play the optimum game, our opponent will also maximum the difference in their favor, so f(i, j) = max({ai - f(i + 1, j), aj - f(i, j -1)}), we see that iteration order is increasing in j and decreasing in i.

notes.note: Wrote f(i,j)=max(a_i - f(i+1,j), a_j - f(i,j-1)) with the folded sign — the exact recurrence and the exact insight (both players run the same optimum game, so one number suffices) — plus the fill order. AC 13:29/55:00, 43/43 hidden, first attempt: 25% of budget. Cleanest problem of the round.

title: LR insertion (AtCoder ABC237 D)
reflection: Stack version works just fine.

past_attempts.approach: I realize one thing, each L and R actions are moving us down a tree, if 'i' has taken 'R' it means i would come after (i - 1) also all the subsequent numbers will also come after (i - 1), so in tree-sense, i is the right-subtree of (i - 1) and we will do pre-order traversal, can be simulated through stack.

notes.note: Chose the tree reduction — i is the L/R child of i-1, final order = in-order traversal — correct but ornate; the needed idea was that every insertion is adjacent to a moving frontier, so reading S backwards into a deque is 5 lines. AC 14:51/15:00 on the OJ, but recursion depth = tree height (N at worst) stack-overflowed the local judge: RE on hidden tests 59/60, the only N=5·10^5 cases. Recognition ornate, implementation fragile at scale.

Repair: found a streaming in-order — stack holds only the current run of 'L' edges, and node i-1 prints the instant you read S[i]=='R' (that char is exactly the label of i-1's edge). One forward pass, no descent phase, no recursion: AC 4:42, 60/60 hidden, hint-free. Simpler than the descent-unwind sketch I'd staged, so the closure came from his own model rather than from being handed the deque.

title: A. Party

approach: In each group there cannot be any superior-subordinate pair, the hierarchy structure is a bunch of trees, considering a single tree and it's longest branch, let's say of height h, then those h employees have to be each in different groups. So there has to be atleast h groups, and we see in these 'h' groups we can fit other branches as well, we do this same exercise for each tree and find the largest(h). I will go for DFS for largest height.

notes.note: Chose the needed reduction unprompted — max root-to-worker chain length, with the "other branches fit in the same h groups" argument — but built child adjacency lists and a recursive DFS for it. The same number falls straight out of the parent array. AC 12:39/11:00 first try, 30/30 hidden, hint-free. Label clean; the cost is machinery, not recognition.

title: ABC146 C - Buy an Integer
reflection: Had to realize that the shop only sells integers upto a limit.
approach: The cost function A*N + d(N)*B = c(N), depends on both the N as well as d(N), both vary at different rates, but we observe a monotonicity, c(N1) < c(N2) if N1 < N2. c(N) becomes infeasible atmost once. We can binary search that.

notes.note: Named monotonicity of A·N + B·d(N) and went straight to binary search on [0, 1e9] with 64-bit cost and the shop ceiling clamped from the start. Exactly the needed reduction. AC 09:31/15:00 first try, 37/37 hidden including the two double-arithmetic killers. Clean.

title: B. Sherlock and his girlfriend
reflection: The time complexity is O(sqrt(N) * log(N)) I guess?
approach: For any pair of numbers (a, b) the color is required to mismatch only if a | b and a is prime. Let's say all the numbers in range are primes, then they can all be of the same color, let's say C1, now if there are other non-prime numbers then they cannot have the same color as C1, so they need C2 and they can all have C2. If all primes, we go with single color C1, if non-primes are there, we need C2, and C2 is sufficient.

notes.note: Best recognition of the round: derived that only (prime, multiple) pairs conflict, so primes get one colour and composites another and k is 1 or 2 — the colouring machinery never appeared. But the sieve is sized N+1 while it writes and reads index N+1: out of bounds by one on every input, invisible because the two accesses land on the same bit and it reads true from vector<bool> word padding. title: C. Cd and pwd commands
reflection: Fairly straight forward implementation.
approach: I need to keep a stack of the current open directory, whenever a command comes in if it's "cd" and starts with "/" I scratch my stack, other wise I append the tokens to it. if any token is ".." then I pop one element from the stack. if the command is "pwd" then I print the stack delimited by "/".

notes.note: Stack of components, cleared on a leading '/', pushed by name, popped on '..', printed with a trailing slash — the exact needed model, stated before coding, and it steps over the splice trap entirely. AC 15:32/26:00 first try, 27/27 hidden, hint-free. Clean.

title: Towers
reflection: Had to figure out the way to keep the towers sorted without having to resort them everytime, the problem was well curated to assist in that.
approach: Since each tower has to be processed in order, let's say we are processing kth tower and we have m (each with top most block a1, a2, a3, a4.. am) towers already, if k cannot be put in any existing tower, then the tower count becomes (m + 1) we have no other choice. but if kth tower can be placed onto ai, aj, ... al blocks we must choose the smallest a. Since (a1, a2, a3 ... am) depicts our capability to accomodate future towers and we have keep them as high as possible. Also if we have a choice we must utlize it. Since the penaly to defer is +1 towers today in favor of averting -1 towers later, so instead of going penalty -> reward, we can go for reward -> penalty if penalty happens it was inevitable.

notes.note: Chose the exact greedy — smallest tower-top strictly greater than the cube — with the exchange argument stated before coding ("defer is +1 today to avert −1 later"). upper_bound on a sorted vector, replaced in place; the sortedness survives because everything before the found top is ≤ b and everything after is > b, so no re-sort is ever needed. AC 11:23/11:00 first try, 27/27 hidden, plus 1500 random cases clean against a Dilworth oracle. Clean.

title: B. The Festive Evening
reflection: Since doors are only 26, sweep + enquiry for each door would also work.
approach: For each gate we know what time they open and what time they close, let's say for each gate the window is [oi, ci] so one guard is needed to watch over that gate in that duration, Since we need multiple range updates followed by a single query, we can work with difference-arrays followed by a sweep and then query.

notes.note: Chose first/last per door plus a difference array and one sweep — the needed model, with a 26-entry counter as the cheaper equivalent (he named that himself in the reflection). Latent smell, not a bug: the 26 letters that never appear each inject a phantom interval [0,1] because fst=last=0, and those cancel exactly at every queried position. Verified on 4000 random cases. AC 07:35/15:00 first try, 51/51 hidden. Clean.

title: D - Knight
reflection: I had to realize that DP won't work, then found pattern with binomial coefficients and then realized a mistake in my formula it's KC(X - K) not (K + 1)C(X - K).
approach: Actual chess knight can jump in all 8 directions, but for this minimal problem, we just need to do a count-dp ensuring the iteration is in increasing order of i and increasing order of j, I will work with push DP. One thing to note though. both X, Y <= 1e6 so if we go iterative way, I am forced to navigate through all the possibilities which will O(XY) and TLE, however I see that starting from (0, 0) to any (x, y) we are only every going if (x + y = 0 mod 3), makes me feel the grid is sparse. So I could iterate it better through recursive implementation, I see that (x, y) for each recursive call is only going to decrease and for each layer if x + y = 3K, there would be K + 1 terms, and this would lead to TLE even with recursive implementation with cache. I do see a pattern though the numbers are binomial coefficients. First I have to check whether it's feasible, which can be checked by (x + y) = 3K and x, y >= K. if yes, then the answer should be (K + 1)C(x - K)

notes.note: Committed to count-DP, priced it at O(XY) = 10^12, tried memoized recursion, priced that too, and only then found the binomial — the right reduction, reached by experiment rather than by reading the constraint line. Final form C(K, X−K) with K=(X+Y)/3 and guards X ≥ K, Y ≥ K, which sidesteps the negative-modulo trap entirely. AC 27:15/21:00 first try, 28/28 hidden; 0.22 s on the largest case. Label slow-recognition — the whole 130% of budget was recognition.

title: B. Han Solo and Lazer Gun
reflection: Handling the horizontal and vertical shoots and the negative values was tricky.
approach: I will always shift the gun to the origin, then every line from the laser would be of form ax + by = 0, which then each tropper position can be uniquely determined by pair (a, b) such that gcd(a, b) = 1, and each such buckets (a, b) can be cleaned up in one shot, so we need to find the number of such pairs (a, b).

notes.note: Shifts the gun to the origin and keys each trooper by (|dx|/g, |dy|/g, sign(dx·dy)), with vertical and horizontal as two separate flags — that triple is exactly one line through the gun, so opposite rays collapse and a vertical never divides. The needed reduction, reached without floats. AC 23:35/25:00 first try, 34/34 hidden. Clean.

title: C. Edgy Trees
reflection: Removing the edges to form isolated blocks and then find the "impact" of those edges is a good heuristic.
approach: whichever path uses the black-edge contributes to the total. Now to find how many paths use the black egde is difficult (atleast I am not able to come up with it). But it's easier to count how many paths don't contain it. Let's consider the tree with the black edges removed, we get multiple isolated components, let's call them blocks, there are say M blocks. If there is a path which remains inside one block, those paths don't need any black edge, but if there is a path which connects to two or more blocks needs black-edge to do so. Again it's easier to count for each block, how many paths remains in that block. if a block is of size l, then number of k-sized-paths is l^k, and we do that for each block and find the total number of paths which are not-valid, we substract that from the total number of paths to get the desired result

notes.note: Chose the complement unprompted in the approach line: delete black edges, each red region of size s contributes s^k bad sequences, answer N^K − Σ s^k. DSU on red edges only, sizes read at roots, mod helpers throughout. AC 10:39/28:00 first try, hint-free, 0 wrong attempts. Clean — recognition and implementation both instant.

title: 080 — Let's Share Bit
reflection: Time complexity is O(2^N * (N + D))

notes.note: Found the complement reduction alone: answer = 2^D − |union of failure sets|, f(S) = 2^(D − popcount(OR)) for the x failing every condition in S, sign (−1)^(|S|+1) derived from the two-set case and checked on {0,4} being double-counted. Argued explicitly against the all-S form and kept the union form with the empty term dropped — a deliberate choice, correct. __builtin_popcountll killed the D factor; OR recomputed per mask O(N). title: Lunar New Year and a Wander
reflection: Had to realize that my greedy suggests "pick the lowest number which is visitable", so it's inherently BFS. I tried first with DFS and picking the lowest number which is available for that particular node. Which went wrong and I realized my implementation was wrong from the test-failures. Greedy had a simpler shape, whichever nodes are reachable now, visit the one with the smallest number.
approach: Since he records the nodes only when it's not been visited once, visiting smaller numbered nodes again and again doesn't give us any smaller lexicographical order. And each point the order is determined at the earliest index of difference, so given the choice we must always try to pick the smallest node to visit first. It's greedy

notes.note: Cold drill AC 14:35 (0 WA, 0 hints, 40/40 hidden): recognized greedy min-next-node upfront, initially tried local-neighbor DFS before sample failures pointed to global frontier min-heap BFS (implementation/shape gap, self-corrected cleanly).

title: Division and Union
reflection: Lost some time in realizing the order has to be preserved while assigning them the group, after sort the indexes got jumbled.
approach: The requirement is that each member of group 1 should be non-intersecting with each element in group 2. There is no limitations of mandate on the intersection-status inside the groups. Let's say there is some element in group-1 which doesn't intersect with any other element within group-1 then it can be moved to group-2, so we can work with group-1 having only the elements which all intersect with each other. So we start with the ranges in increasing order of li and then we start checking intersection of the kth-range with group-1 so far (group-1 cannot be empty so first range has to add regardless). if there is intersection they have to the group-1, if there is no intersection with the group-1 we move it to group-2 and we are found the partition.

notes.note: Cold drill AC 29:27 (0 WA, 0 hints, 35/35 hidden): immediately derived sort-by-l + prefix max-r gap check upfront; lost a couple minutes tracking original indices after sorting (implementation detail).

title: Cut 'em all!
reflection: Had a bug in taking inputs, I was taking input for number of nodes and number of edges, when the problem was only providing the number of nodes.
approach: Took me some time to figure out. First things, if the tree / subtree has odd-number of vertices we cannot split it. Also after a valid split, each vertex will be a part of some component, so I can start my search with any vertex as parent and will be able to arrive at each possible split. So I will start from parent, lets call that root, node 1. now for each child I will ask if it's splittable, splittable means if the subtree is of even size. If it's of even size, then I will collect the number of ways to split that child and add 1 to it. Here after splitting the component containing the parent will remain valid, because root contains even number of vertices 2m, and we will only split the child if had even number of vertices, 2k, so 2m - 2k = 2 (m - k), let's call this subtree (parent without subtree) pwc, will still leave the pwc with even number of terms. so whenever a substree has even number of vertices I cut it loose immediately, because if there was some larger split possible with the with was working with parent (pwc + subtree), it will still work, and by splitting parent into pwc + subtree I gain one further cut. Cutting a valid subtree loose doesn't invalidate any valid cuts for the parent. So in my DFS order whenever I encounter a even-number of component in the subtree I am in I will cut count it and the number of cuts will be one-less-than-that.

notes.note: Cold drill AC 42:29 (0 WA, 0 hints, 35/35 hidden): derived exact even-subtree cut invariance ($2m - 2k = 2(m-k)$) upfront and implemented clean DFS subtree parity count; extra time split between deriving the tree greedy and reading an extra M in input.

title: Nested Segments
reflection: Got to know by a failing test case that, while sorting by increasing li, gives me a clear range to look for candidates (to the right) I should so sort by rj in decreasing manner so as to capture the "domination" of the candidate. Since I am validating if the current range is dominating all the candidates to the right, all the elements which it can possibly dominate should be to it's right, sort by li does that job for left-edge, for the right edge we need to sort secondarily by decreasing order of rj.
approach: Tough. I need to honor two conditions. for a pair i, j. They need to honor li <= lj and ri >= rj. So my first thought is to sort the ranges by li, so li <= lj requirement is trivially met, just checking if the index lies to the right. For each index i, I will need to check all the rj's to the right of i, and find the smallest rj, since rj >= li (because rj >= lj >= li) I just need to compare the smallest rj so far to the right with ri, if that lies within we met the second requirement as well, otherwise if even the earliest-closing (minimum rj) is after ri, then there is no domination done by current range at i.

notes.note: Cold drill AC 27:16 (0 WA, 0 hints, 36/36 hidden): sorted by l asc, r desc and checked adjacent r[i] >= r[i+1]; reflection caught the equal-l tie-break (r desc) after a failing test.

title: Minimize the error (water-level)
reflection: Accepted, surprisingly the execution time is higher. 31 ms for simulation and 46 ms for binary search. It's not surprising now taht I think about it. since K1 + K2 <= 1000 and both solutions are O(NlogN)

past_attempts.approach: Since we only care about the sum of squares and we are allowed to both increment and decrement the values, for each deli = ai - bi, we will use the operations to move the deli towards zero, |deli| will reduce. which will decrease square(deli), since the operations are limited we must use it first to decrement |deli| which gives us the most returns, and the returns are exactly (deli)^2 - (deli - 1)^2 = 2 * deli - 1, since we have to take exactly K1 + K2 operations it's possible we may worsen the error after some point. even in that case we must go with decreasing order of deli. It only matters that we perform (K1 + K2) operations in total since any +1/-1 operation on ai can be translated to -1/+1 operation on bi. So we merely need to perform exactly K1 + K2 operations in total.

notes.note: Cold drill AC 22:28 (0 WA, 0 hints, 45/45 hidden): reduced to K=k1+k2 moves on |a_i-b_i| via max-heap using marginal gain 2d-1; abs(curr-1) handles the 0->1->0 parity bounce cleanly. Reflection caught signed vs |diff_i| ordering.

approach: For each connected component, i.e. friend circle, is always optimal to send rumor through the cheapest friend. Because others in the friend-circle will get the rumor for free. So all we need to do is go through each component (could be a single friend) and find the minimum in that component. I will employ DSU for this.

title: CF332B - Maximum Absurdity
reflection: Good implementation problem had to take care of prefix, suffix, max-override. Not tough but good practice.
approach: We need to select two non-intersecting k-sized subarrays with maximum sum, so we can work with prefix and suffix of the array, that guarantees non-intersecting, Now given a range we need to find out the maximum k-sized subarray sum encountered so far, which can be easily maintained with prefix-sum and a running-winner. for each index i, we will work with max-winner-prefix(i) and max-winner-suffix(i + 1) and find the maximum total value, to honor the output format we will keep the running-winner values of smallest index for prefix and suffix. This should work fine. We will pre-compute the max-winner-* before hand and then iterate to find and construct the solution.

notes.note: ThemeCP L17 P4 AC 23:50 (0 WA, 34/34): clean prefix/suffix k-window decomposition with exact tie-breaking (< forward, <= backward, > combine) and 64-bit sums.

title: ABC116 C - Grand Garden
reflection: Good eye spotting, the simulation was reducing to this elegant observation. if the target immediately to the left is larger or greater than current, target[i - 1] >= target[i], the range [l, r] which included i - 1, could have included i as well until target of i is reached, so i gets a free ride, only when the target for i is greater than target[i - 1] is when we have pay for additional sweeps. This looks skewed towards the (i - 1, i) comparison, but the same observation will hold if we work with (i, i + 1) as well comparing target[i] > target[i + 1], working with fixed r in [l, r] instead of fixed l in [l, r] in previous reasoning.

past_attempts.approach: If the flowers were allowed all exceed their targets we can always just water them all and all reach the max({hi}) height. However the requirement is strict. So we realize that once the target is reached for certain flowers they shouldn't be touched anymore, and essentially they split the range into parts, for each valid part we need to apply the sweep of maximal [l, r] given that all values in [l, r] are greater than 0. since h <= 100, we can simulate this.

notes.note: ThemeCP L17 P1 AC 10:50 (0 WA, 29/29): recognized zero-split structure upfront and simulated height sweeps O(N*max(h)); equivalent to O(N) upward-step sum max(0, h_i - h_{i-1}).

title: CF574B - Bear and Three Musketeers
reflection: Got stuck into nasty bug where I was trying for all pairs of (a, b), but I need to check that (a, b) are direct acquaintances.
approach: This problem is about realizing that brute force is good enough, because the asymptotic computations despite looking ugle come upto O(N^2) which should be doable within limits. For each pair of the (a, b), we will go through their acquintances and if both a & b have them as common we consider their result. For a particular a with all different b, (a, _) => the computations requires are sum-of-degress = 2 * N. So each (a, *) is O(N), now we loop over all a, this will make the total computations to be O(N^2).

title: Three Strings
reflection: Peculiar problem, good realization on the order and state redundancy.
approach: We need to figure out the number of disagreements which are happening between c and (a, b) basically minimizing the number of indexes where 'c' cannot have formed by having interleaving of a and b. We can work with f(i, j, k) = minimum number of disagreements when considering the first i characters of a, first j of b and first k of c. If c[k] matches a[i], then we can consider consulting f(i - 1, j, k -1), if c[k] matches b[j] then we can consider f(i, j - 1, k - 1), if we don't want to / can't match with any we can consider there was some overlapping and choose between min(f(i - 1, j, k - 1), f(i, j - 1, k - 1)) + 1. Now since |a|, |b| <= 1000 we can't have O(N^3) neither in space nor time, so we realize that i + j == k always, so we can move k to be derived value from i, j, we move to state (i, j) = f(i, j) = minimum number of disagrements of first i characters of a, first j characters of b with first (i + j) characters of c. we have to iterate in the increasing order k, i.e. as it is a valid order. so increasing order of (i + j).

title: Pride
reflection: Took my quite some time in discovering the solution. Not dissatisfied with my implementation.
approach: Took me quite some time to come up with idea, if all gcd(..all numbers..) > 1, then it's impossible, if gcd(ai) (i = 1, N) = 1, then it's possible, we want to achieve gcd = 1 as soon as possible in the chain of the gcd(ak, gcd(al, ... gcd(am, an)) because once gcd is found at the kth later, then we have to pay the extra to make those k layers 1 as well. Let's say we got a 1 in our array, then the number of operations needed after that is N - 1, which is fixed, in fact if there are k 1's then we require exactly N - k operations. So we must operate in such a way to obtain our first 1 as soon as possible, for this we can just iterate over all the ranges and find the smallest range which gives the gcd as 1, N <= 2000 so O(N^2) is doable.

title: ABC147 D - Xor Sum 4
reflection: Had to realize that inputs have to be long long, needed a few minutes of debugging for this.
approach: If we consider ai ^ aj = ak when we expand across it's bits ak = k1 * 2^m1 + k2 * 2^m2 + k3 * 2^m3 .... Where each m1, m2, m3 is independently derivable by XOR'ing the mth bit of ai ^ aj. So each ai ^ aj, is nothing but expansion of the sum where each term is independently determined by bitwise XOR. For each mi, we need to find out the sum of ki across all the pairs. We realize that the if the mi'th bit of ai and aj are both 0, or both 1, they contribute 0 towards ki, but if they're different they contribute 1 towards ki. So for each bit position mi, we need to find out how many bits are set to zero, n0, and how many bits are set to 1, n1, then ki will be equal to n0 * n1. So the mi'th bit will contribute (n0 * n1) * 2^mi to the total sum. We will go bitwise.

title: C. Kuroni and Impossible Calculation
reflection: Good learning this problem, modular arithmetic doesn't penetrate the "abs" function, also doesn't work on the exponent of the a^b, but works with the base.
approach: We need to realize that (a1 * a2 * a3 * ... ) mod M = (a1 mod M * a2 mod M * a3 mod M * ...) mod M. So a1, a2, a3... etc can have m buckets. Since a1 = numsi - numsj, which again allows modular distribution. numsi and numsj also belong to M buckets, if there are two numbers in the same bucket, the product drops to zero and pigeon hole principle guarantees that if N > M, there would be two numsi and numsj which would fall into the same bucket, lending the entire product to zero. So if N > M, we print zero, otherwise we can brute force the product, since N <= M <= 1000 which is doable.

past_attempts.approach: The multiplication is required for all pairs (i < j) and with absolute value |ai - aj|, since it's absolute value the order doesn't matterand since we are finding the difference for all pair. Also i notice that the mod 'm' m <= 1000. So I can reduce all the numbers of their remainder modded with m. So instead of having N numbers I will have m buckets, each bucket bi will be filled by ci number of numbers. Now I can iterate over all the mi, mj, for the difference (mi - mj) mod m. And the number of pairs contributing this to the product would be ci * cj. So for each i, j, we will contribute ((mi - mj) mod m)^ (ci * cj). I will sum it over for all the i, j <= 1000
